A science and history lesson · The planet Mars

Exploring Mars: Past, Present and Future

From Schiaparelli’s “canali” to Perseverance’s sample tubes, and the sites, budgets, rockets and rules that will decide what happens next, with five maps drawn from spacecraft data

Prepared by Scholar · October 2026

This lesson follows human attempts to understand and reach Mars: the telescope observers and the mistaken “canals” of the 1800s, the first spacecraft of the 1960s and 1970s, the rovers and orbiters of the last three decades, the state of exploration on 27 October 2026, and the plans, proposed landing sites and legal rules that shape what comes next. It uses five maps drawn from public elevation data (MOLA), so each place can be seen where it lies on the planet.

The facts about the present and future were checked against sources read on 27 October 2026, and each claim is attributed. Items that I could not confirm in a second source are marked [unconfirmed]. Company and national timelines that are goals and not approved, funded schedules are marked [aspirational]. Technical words are explained when they first appear. The photographs are public-domain files from NASA or Wikimedia Commons.

1The lesson

Mars, from the telescope to the sample tube

Seven sections · about 80–100 minutes · 5 maps, 12 images, a timeline, a link to NASA’s Mars Trek and 10 review questions · facts as of 27 October 2026

1. Mars in brief, and how to read the maps

Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun. Its mean radius is 3,389.5 kilometers, so its diameter is about 6,779 kilometers, a little more than half of Earth’s. Gravity at the equator is 3.71 meters per second squared, about 38 percent of Earth’s. The air is about 95 percent carbon dioxide, and the average pressure at the surface is about 610 pascals, roughly 0.6 percent of Earth’s sea-level pressure (NASA Mars Fact Sheet; NASA JPL Planetary Physical Parameters). A person on the surface would need a pressure suit, not only a mask.

A day on Mars is called a sol. It lasts about 24 hours and 39 minutes. A Martian year is about 687 Earth days. Radio signals between Earth and Mars take roughly 3 to 22 minutes in one direction, depending on where the two planets are in their orbits. Because the planets line up well for a launch only about once every 26 months, missions leave in groups called launch windows: 2020 was one, and late 2026 is another (Japan’s MMX probe left on 20 October 2026).

Coordinates used in this course

Every map uses the planetocentric latitude, which is the angle between a point on the surface, the center of Mars, and the equator. (The older planetographic latitude measures the angle from the local vertical instead; the two differ by up to a fraction of a degree at middle latitudes.) Longitude is measured east-positive from the prime meridian, which is defined by a small crater named Airy-0. The U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) lists longitudes from 0° to 360° east. Each map in this course says on its face which labels it uses, and the same place can be written two ways: Olympus Mons, for example, is at 226.2°E, which is also 133.8°W. Some older sources, including NASA’s own page for Viking 1, give planetographic west longitudes, so the same place can have two very different-looking numbers. The word areocentric means “centered on Mars” (from Ares, the Greek name for the planet’s god), and it is the Mars counterpart of “geocentric”.

Elevation on Mars has no sea level to start from. Scientists use a reference surface called the MOLA datum instead. It is based on a model of the planet’s gravity field and mean radius, and elevations on the maps are measured above or below it. The data come from the Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA), a laser instrument on NASA’s Mars Global Surveyor orbiter (1997 to 2006). The global grid used here has a cell size of about 463 meters. Its published vertical uncertainty is at least ±3 meters, and the data are sparse beyond 87° latitude (USGS Astropedia; public domain).

Two features to know before anything else

Mars has a lopsided shape. Most of the northern hemisphere is a low, smooth plain, and most of the southern hemisphere is high and heavily cratered. In the west, near the equator, a huge volcanic region called Tharsis rises above both. It holds the three Tharsis Montes volcanoes (Arsia, Pavonis and Ascraeus), the giant Olympus Mons to their northwest, and the chasms of Valles Marineris to their east. The map in Figure 1 shows this region with the USGS names and centers.

Olympus Mons is the tallest known volcano in the Solar System. Published heights differ with the data and the datum used: the 463-meter MOLA grid I measured peaks at 21,241 meters, and reference works often quote about 22 kilometers. Valles Marineris is a canyon system about 3,761 kilometers long according to the USGS gazetteer. The two photographs below show both features.

Two more terms help. Regolith means the loose layer of dust, sand and broken rock that covers most of the surface; Mars has no soil in the biological sense. In-situ resource utilization (ISRU) means making something useful, such as oxygen or water, from materials at the destination instead of carrying it from Earth. Both words come back in section 7.

Key dates
  1. 3,389.5 kmMean radius of Mars (NASA/JPL)
  2. 3.71 m/s²Equatorial gravity
  3. ~610 PaAverage surface pressure
  4. ~26 monthsInterval between good launch windows
Why it matters

Almost every plan in this course is a response to the numbers above. The thin air makes parachutes weak and makes landing heavy spacecraft hard. The long radio delay means rovers must make many decisions alone. The wide time gaps between launch windows make every failure expensive in time as well as money.

Explore Mars yourself

Mars Trek is a free NASA web portal. It lets you view and combine map layers of data from Mars spacecraft, switch between a flat map, polar maps and a 3D globe, and measure distances and elevations. Its Data menu (read on 27 October 2026) lists landing-site markers for Viking 1 and 2, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Phoenix, Curiosity, InSight and Perseverance; MOLA elevation layers, which come from the same laser-altimeter data as this course’s maps but are processed differently; a layer named “Perseverance (Mars 2020) Path”; and “Exploration Zones” layers. I did not check how current the path layer is, so compare it with Figure 13, and note that layer lists can change.

2. Before spacecraft: telescopes and the canal error

Mars is easy to find because it is bright and red. Galileo pointed a small telescope at it in 1610, but he could not see surface detail. In 1659 the Dutch astronomer Christiaan Huygens drew a dark triangular marking now called Syrtis Major, and in the 1660s Giovanni Cassini and others followed dark and light features and noticed white polar caps. Over the next two centuries observers learned that Mars turns once in a little over 24 hours and that its caps grow and shrink with the seasons (Sheehan, The Planet Mars, 1996).

The year 1877 was a close approach, which astronomers call an opposition (Earth passes between Mars and the Sun). That August the American astronomer Asaph Hall discovered Mars’s two small moons, Phobos and Deimos. The same year, in Milan, Giovanni Schiaparelli sketched a network of thin dark lines that he called canali. The Italian word means “channels”. English-language reports translated it as “canals”, a word that suggests something dug by people. Figure 4 shows his map of 1888.

The American businessman and astronomer Percival Lowell took the idea much further. He founded the Lowell Observatory at Flagstaff, Arizona, in 1894 and published books, including Mars and Its Canals (1906), which argued that the lines were irrigation works built by an intelligent, dying civilization to carry water from the polar caps. Lowell’s drawings, such as the one in Figure 5, showed hundreds of fine lines that joined at dark spots.

The canals were not real. Other astronomers of the time doubted them. The naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace argued in 1907 that Mars was too cold and dry for Lowell’s picture, and in 1909 the Greek-born French astronomer Eugène Antoniadi used a large telescope at Meudon, near Paris, and saw irregular patches where Lowell had drawn straight lines (Sheehan 1996). Later accounts explain the error as a mix of blurring by Earth’s atmosphere, the eye’s tendency to join faint spots into lines, and the observers’ expectations. No spacecraft has ever found a canal network. Section 3 describes the first close look, which settled the question.

Spectroscopy, which splits starlight into colors to identify gases, added knowledge in the 1900s. In 1947 Gerard Kuiper detected carbon dioxide in the Martian air (Sheehan 1996). Estimates of the surface pressure made from Earth, however, were many times higher than the true value that Mariner 4 later measured, and some astronomers still thought that the seasonal dark patches might be plants. These guesses were corrected by spacecraft within a few years.

Key dates
  1. 1610Galileo observes Mars with a telescope
  2. 1877Schiaparelli’s “canali”; Hall finds Phobos and Deimos
  3. 1894Lowell Observatory founded at Flagstaff
  4. 1909Antoniadi sees no canals at Meudon
  5. 1947Kuiper detects CO₂ in the air
Why it matters

The canal story is a clear case of observers seeing what they expected. It is also the reason that later missions were built to measure the planet with instruments, not to rely on human impressions. When a result is exciting, as the Cheyava Falls sample is in section 5, the lesson of the canals is to ask what other tests could confirm it.

3. The first spacecraft and the Cold War

The first attempts to reach Mars began in 1960. The Soviet Union launched several probes in 1960 and 1962, and the United States launched Mariner 3 in 1964; all of these failed, some at launch and some on the way (NASA NSSDCA). Success came with Mariner 4, launched on 28 November 1964. It flew past Mars on 14 and 15 July 1965 at a closest distance of 9,846 kilometers. It took 21 pictures and part of a 22nd, covering about 1 percent of the surface, and returned a total of 5.2 million bits of data. A bit is the smallest unit of digital data; 5.2 million bits is about 650 kilobytes, less than one photograph from a modern phone (my conversion; NASA NSSDCA, 1964-077A).

The pictures showed craters like those on the Moon. Radio signals that passed through the Martian air before reaching Earth gave a surface pressure of 4.1 to 7.0 millibars and found no magnetic field. Many people had expected a more Earth-like planet, and the result changed the public image of Mars from a possible home of life to a cold, dry and cratered world. According to NASA’s description of the item, staff at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) did not wait for the computers to process the first data and colored a printout of the numbers by hand. Figure 6 shows that printout and Figure 7 the finished image.

Mariner 6 and 7 flew past in July and August 1969 and photographed more of the surface, again with little change in the overall picture (NASA NSSDCA). Then came a change. Mariner 9, launched on 30 May 1971, reached Mars on 14 November 1971 and became the first spacecraft to orbit another planet. A global dust storm had begun in September and hid most of the surface; at first only the summits of Olympus Mons and the three Tharsis volcanoes stood above the dust. As the dust cleared, Mariner 9 returned 7,329 images that covered the whole planet. They showed the huge volcanoes, the great canyon (named Valles Marineris in its honor), dry riverbed-like channels and the polar caps, and gave the first close views of Phobos and Deimos. Mariner 9 was turned off on 27 October 1972 (NASA NSSDCA, 1971-051A). Mariner 8, its twin, had failed at launch.

The Soviet attempts

The Soviet Union sent two large spacecraft, Mars 2 and Mars 3, in 1971. Each carried an orbiter and a lander. The Mars 2 lander crashed on 27 November 1971 [unconfirmed]. The Mars 3 lander touched down on 2 December 1971 and was the first spacecraft to land softly on Mars. It stopped transmitting after a very short time. Standard accounts give 14.5 seconds (NASA) or about 20 seconds (reports in 1971); a 2024 Russian analysis argues that the signal lasted at least 62 seconds (Rocket-Space Instrument Engineering, 2024). The cause of the loss is unknown; a planet-wide dust storm that was then in progress is a leading explanation (NASA Solar System Exploration). Mars 6 and Mars 7 were launched in 1973 and arrived in 1974. The Mars 6 lander lost contact during its descent, and the Mars 7 lander missed the planet [unconfirmed]. The landing positions of Mars 2 and 3 on the maps are approximate, because the sources I could check give only rounded values.

Viking

NASA’s Viking project sent two spacecraft, each with an orbiter and a lander, in August and September 1975. Viking 1’s lander separated from its orbiter on 20 July 1976 and landed in western Chryse Planitia at 22.27°N, 312.05°E (planetocentric) at 11:53 UTC. It sent its first surface picture 25 seconds after landing. Viking 1’s lander worked until contact was lost on 13 November 1982 (NASA NSSDCA, 1975-075C). Viking 2 landed on 3 September 1976 in Utopia Planitia, and its lander worked until April 1980 (the April 1980 date is from memory of the NASA record and was not re-checked for this lesson) [unconfirmed]. The whole project cost roughly $1 billion in the money of the time.

The landers carried three experiments to look for microbes. One of them, called Labeled Release, gave a result that looked like biological activity. The other instrument, which searched for organic (carbon-based) molecules in the soil, found none at the detection level at the two sites. Most scientists concluded that the result was chemical, not biological. In 2010 a study suggested that perchlorate (a reactive salt later confirmed on Mars) could have destroyed organic molecules when the soil was heated, which would have hidden them (Navarro-González et al. 2010). The question is therefore described by most researchers as unresolved but unlikely to show life, and a small number of the original investigators still argue otherwise. This course takes the first view and labels it as the majority one.

The “Great Galactic Ghoul”

By the 1970s engineers were joking about a space monster that ate Mars-bound spacecraft, nicknamed the “Great Galactic Ghoul”. The nickname fitted the record: many early Mars missions failed, and the failures kept coming in the 1990s. NASA’s history office credits the phrase to JPL’s John Casani, while a different account credits the Time magazine writer Donald Neff; the origin is disputed (NASA History). Counts of how many missions have failed differ with what is counted, so I give no single percentage.

Key dates
  1. 28 Nov 1964Mariner 4 launched
  2. 14–15 Jul 1965Mariner 4 flyby: 21 images
  3. 14 Nov 1971Mariner 9 enters Mars orbit
  4. 2 Dec 1971Mars 3: first soft landing; very short signal
  5. 20 Jul 1976Viking 1 lands
  6. 3 Sep 1976Viking 2 lands
  7. 13 Nov 1982Last contact with Viking 1 lander
Why it matters

In under twelve years the picture of Mars changed three times: from a possible home of life and canals, to a dead and cratered world, to a planet with giant volcanoes, a canyon, and riverlike channels. The Viking results also set the standard question that every later mission has asked: where was liquid water, and did it leave signs of life?

4. The long return, 1996 to 2021

After Viking, no spacecraft reached Mars for about 17 years. NASA’s Mars Observer, launched in 1992, lost contact in August 1993 just before it was to enter orbit, and a Russian mission, Mars 96, failed at launch in 1996. In late 1996 two new missions left Earth. The result was the start of an almost continuous presence at Mars, which the map below summarizes: every known landing and crash site, colored by who sent it and marked by when it flew and how it ended.

1997 to 2008: orbiters, the first rovers, and ice

Mars Pathfinder landed on 4 July 1997 inside inflated air bags and released Sojourner, the first wheeled rover on another planet. Sojourner was about the size of a microwave oven and stayed within a short distance of the lander, but it showed that a rover could work on Mars (NASA NSSDCA). Pathfinder’s last transmission was on 27 September 1997.

Mars Global Surveyor reached Mars in September 1997 and mapped the planet until it lost contact in November 2006. It carried the MOLA laser altimeter, whose data produced the elevation maps in this course, and a magnetometer that found strong patches of magnetized rock in the old southern crust, a sign that Mars once had a global magnetic field (Acuña et al. 1999). Mars Odyssey, which arrived in October 2001 and is still operating, found in 2002 large amounts of hydrogen just under the surface near the poles. Researchers interpreted this as water ice (NASA JPL).

Two of NASA’s 1999 missions failed. The Mars Climate Orbiter was lost on 23 September 1999 because one team’s software supplied thruster data in English units (pound-seconds) while the navigation software expected metric units (newton-seconds), and the craft entered the atmosphere too low. The Mars Polar Lander and the two small Deep Space 2 probes were lost on 3 December 1999. A review board found that the lander’s legs probably caused a false “landed” signal, which shut down the engines about 40 meters above the ground (NASA Science; NASA LLIS).

The European Space Agency (ESA) launched its first Mars spacecraft, Mars Express, which entered orbit in December 2003. It carried a small British lander, Beagle 2, which was dropped on 25 December 2003 and never reported. In January 2015 NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter photographed it on the surface, showing that it had landed but that its solar panels had not fully opened (NASA/UK Space Agency).

In January 2004 NASA’s twin rovers Spirit and Opportunity landed on opposite sides of the planet. They were built to last 90 sols, and lasted years. Opportunity found rocks at Meridiani Planum that formed in the presence of liquid water, which was acidic and salty at times (Squyres et al. 2004). Spirit’s last contact was on 22 March 2010, and NASA ended its recovery attempts in May 2011. Opportunity’s last contact was on 10 June 2018, during a global dust storm; NASA declared the mission complete on 13 February 2019, after the rover had driven 45.16 kilometers (NASA JPL). The 2006 arrival of Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO) added the HiRISE camera, which can pick out objects about one meter across from orbit. In 2008 Phoenix landed in the far north at 68.22°N and confirmed water ice under the soil, and its chemistry instrument found perchlorate salts (NASA JPL).

2012 to 2018: a laboratory on wheels, and an atmosphere that escaped

Curiosity, the Mars Science Laboratory, landed in Gale crater on 6 August 2012 (UTC; 5 August in California) using a “sky crane”, a rocket platform that lowered the rover on cables. It is about the size of a small car. In its first year it found a dry lake bed at Yellowknife Bay with chemistry that could have supported microbes (Grotzinger et al. 2014). It has since climbed Mount Sharp, a mound of layered rock in the crater’s center, reading the planet’s history from the layers.

In September 2014 two orbiters arrived within two days of each other. NASA’s MAVEN (22 September) studied how the upper air escapes into space, and estimated that loss to space played a major part in Mars’s change from a wetter climate to the present dry one (Jakosky et al. 2018). India’s Mangalyaan (Mars Orbiter Mission, 24 September) made India the first country to reach Mars orbit on its first attempt, and the first Asian nation to do so (ISRO). It was built as a technology demonstrator and later lost contact in 2022 [unconfirmed].

The European–Russian ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) reached orbit on 19 October 2016. Its demonstration lander, Schiaparelli, crashed the same day after its on-board computer misjudged its height and released the parachute too early; the crash site is marked on the map (ESA inquiry). NASA’s InSight landed on 26 November 2018 and recorded 1,319 marsquakes before it lost power and the mission ended on 21 December 2022. Its largest quake, on 4 May 2022, had an estimated magnitude of 5 (NASA). Using these seismic waves, scientists found that Mars has a liquid core with a radius of about 1,830 kilometers, which is a little over half of the planet’s radius (Stähler et al. 2021).

2020 to 2021: three missions in one window

Three missions launched in July 2020 and arrived in February 2021. The Emirates Mars Mission, called Hope, built by the United Arab Emirates with U.S. university help, entered orbit on 9 February 2021 and studies the weather and upper air through the whole Martian day. China’s Tianwen-1 entered orbit on 10 February 2021, and on 14 May 2021 (UTC) its Zhurong rover landed in southern Utopia Planitia, making China the second country to land and operate a spacecraft on Mars (CNSA).

NASA’s Perseverance rover landed in Jezero crater on 18 February 2021. It carried a small helicopter, Ingenuity, which made the first powered flight on another planet on 19 April 2021 and flew 72 times before it was damaged and the mission ended on 25 January 2024 (NASA JPL). Perseverance is the first part of a plan to collect rock samples for return to Earth, and its work is the subject of the next section.

Why it matters

Between 1997 and 2021 the question changed from “is there water?” to “where was the water, for how long, and was it habitable?”. Orbiters mapped minerals and ice, rovers read rock layers, and the 2020s missions brought three more countries to Mars. The map shows how the surface missions cluster in a belt near the equator and at a few northern sites, mainly because of sunlight, safety and elevation. That pattern also shapes the choice of future human landing zones in section 6.

5. Mars today, as of 27 October 2026

This section reports what I could confirm on 27 October 2026. Where a statement rests on a press summary, amateur tracking or a funding document that I could not match to a second source, it is marked [unconfirmed]. Status can change quickly, and a budget request is a proposal, not a decision.

What is operating

On the surface (NASA). Curiosity has worked in Gale crater for more than 14 years and reached an elevation gain of 1 kilometer on Mount Sharp on 26 August 2026 (NASA JPL). Perseverance is in its extended mission, which NASA says begins in October 2026 and continues the exploration of the crater rim through about the end of 2028 (NASA Science). On sol 2006 (11 October 2026) its odometry passed 45.22 kilometers, more than Opportunity’s 45.16 kilometers, making it the rover that has driven the farthest on another world (NASA/JPL, 12 October 2026). At that time it was working in an area called Lac de Charmes, west of the crater rim, and heading for a site called Idubi, where light-colored boulders may be a kind of rock called breccia (a mix of broken fragments) that may be older than the crater itself (NASA Science).

In orbit. NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter and Mars Odyssey are operating, according to NASA’s April 2026 presentations to its Mars advisory group (MEPAG). ESA’s ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter is healthy and active (ESA, EPSC 2026 abstract), and ESA’s Mars Express, in orbit since 2003, was extended again in June 2026; its funding is secure to the end of 2026 and a further extension to 2029 has been proposed [unconfirmed]. The UAE’s Hope was extended through 2028 (announced on 17 February 2026) and has returned more than 10 terabytes of data (The National; WAM). China’s Tianwen-1 orbiter was reported working in May 2026 by the Chinese space agency; amateur trackers, including Daniel Estévez, reported a gap in its signal in December 2025, its return in March 2026 and a short safe-mode event on 2 August 2026 [unconfirmed]. The Zhurong rover has been in planned hibernation since May 2022, and no end of mission has been announced.

Ended. NASA’s MAVEN was last heard from on 6 December 2025 after a spacecraft anomaly, and NASA declared the mission ended on 3 June 2026. India’s Mangalyaan is silent [unconfirmed]. InSight and Ingenuity are finished.

On the way. Japan’s Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) probe launched on 20 October 2026. It is to reach Mars orbit in August 2027, land on the moon Phobos around 2030 and return a sample around 2031 (JAXA). NASA’s two small ESCAPADE orbiters, launched in November 2025, are to pass Earth again in November 2026 and reach Mars in about September 2027 (NASA). All dates for spacecraft still in flight are plans.

Main science results

Water in the past. Curiosity found a former lake bed. Perseverance found that Jezero held a lake fed by a river that left a delta, and that the crater floor is made of volcanic rock altered by water (Mangold et al. 2021; Farley et al. 2022). Orbital data show widespread clay and salt minerals, which form in water.

Organic molecules. Organic here means carbon-based; it does not mean “alive”, because organic molecules also form in space and in rocks. In 2018 Curiosity reported organic matter preserved in mudstones about 3 billion years old (Eigenbrode et al. 2018). In 2025 a team led by Caroline Freissinet reported long carbon-chain molecules, decane, undecane and dodecane, in a drilled mudstone sample; the authors say they could come from either non-living chemistry or biology (Freissinet et al. 2025).

Cheyava Falls. In July 2024 Perseverance examined a rock at a place named Cheyava Falls, which showed a pattern of small pale spots with dark rims, nicknamed “leopard spots”. The sample from it, named Sapphire Canyon, was the 25th sample the rover collected. In September 2025 a team led by Joel Hurowitz published in Nature that the rock contained organic carbon with two iron minerals (vivianite and greigite) arranged in a way that, on Earth, can be produced by microbes eating organic matter; they stress that the same minerals can also form without life, and that the rover data show no sign of the high heat or acid that would be needed for the non-living route (Hurowitz et al. 2025; NASA). NASA called this a “potential biosignature”, which means a feature that might indicate past life but needs further study. The firm test is to bring the sample to a laboratory on Earth.

The methane debate. Methane is a gas that on Earth is mostly made by life, though it can also be made by chemistry in rocks. Curiosity’s laser instrument has reported a small seasonal “background” of about 0.4 parts per billion with occasional higher spikes (Webster et al. 2018). The European Trace Gas Orbiter, which can measure methane in the whole air column, found no methane above a very low limit in its first measurements (Korablev et al. 2019). Other researchers have proposed that methane seeping from the ground at Gale could vary during the day (Moores et al. 2019; Ortiz et al. 2024), and a 2025 study questioned the reliability of Curiosity’s detections (Viscardy et al. 2025). I did not find a settled answer.

Inside and above. InSight showed that Mars has a crust, a mantle and a liquid core. MAVEN found a continuing escape of the air to space, and Hope and TGO study the weather and the layers of gas. China’s Zhurong reported signs of water-related minerals in dunes [unconfirmed].

Mars Sample Return and the budget

Mars Sample Return (MSR) is a plan to bring the tubes Perseverance has filled to Earth for study. In 2023 an independent review board found the plan then in place would cost $8 billion to $11 billion and return the samples in about 2040 (NASA). In January 2025 NASA began studying two cheaper options, estimated at $6.6 billion to $7.7 billion and $5.8 billion to $7.1 billion, using a smaller lander (NASA). No option was selected. In January 2026 the U.S. spending law for fiscal year 2026 (H.R. 6938, signed 23 January 2026) stated that it “does not support the existing MSR program” and provided $110 million for “Mars Future Missions” (from summaries of the law; I did not re-read the bill text for this lesson) [unconfirmed].

The President’s Budget Request for fiscal year 2027, released in April 2026, would cut NASA’s total to $18.8 billion, 23 percent below the $24.4 billion enacted for fiscal year 2026, and Planetary Science to $1.876 billion, a cut of 26 percent. It repeats the cancellation of MSR, and keeps the $110 million line for Mars Future Missions. It reduces funding for Perseverance, from $87.5 million in the fiscal year 2024 operating plan to $38.0 million, which would slow its operation. It continues support for Curiosity, MRO and the Trace Gas Orbiter. It does not mention Mars Odyssey, the U.S. role in Mars Express or the U.S. contribution to the European Rosalind Franklin rover, which the American Astronomical Society reads as another proposal to end them (American Astronomical Society summary, 8 April 2026). It also describes a low-cost Mars mission solicitation in October 2026, aimed at a 2030 launch with a cost cap of $220 million, not counting the rocket. Congress writes the final budget, and has often changed such requests, so none of these is a decision.

NASA has also awarded Blue Origin a contract of about $700 million for a Mars Telecommunications Orbiter, a relay satellite to serve future landers; the award faces a protest at the U.S. Government Accountability Office, with a decision due by 21 December 2026 (press reports) [unconfirmed]. NASA now describes Mars as a “horizon goal” (NASA release 26-025).

Key dates
  1. 11 Oct 2026 (sol 2006)Perseverance passes Opportunity’s 45.16 km record
  2. 26 Aug 2026Curiosity reaches 1 km elevation gain on Mount Sharp
  3. 3 Jun 2026NASA ends MAVEN
  4. 23 Jan 2026U.S. FY2026 spending law: MSR not supported
  5. 20 Oct 2026Japan’s MMX launches
  6. 21 Dec 2026Expected date of GAO decision on the relay-orbiter award
Why it matters

The scientific story is at a turning point. The best candidate signs of ancient life are now in sample tubes on Mars that cannot be tested with the instruments the rover carries. At the same time, the American budget request would reduce or end several Mars missions, including the plan to bring the samples home. Whether the tubes are ever returned will be decided by budgets and by competing programs, not by science alone.

6. Where next: sites and plans

This section lists the places on Mars that people have proposed to visit and the programs that might go there. It separates three things that are easy to confuse: approved missions (a spacecraft is built or launched), studied candidates (scientists or engineers wrote papers about a place) and aspirations (a company or agency states a goal without an approved budget). Each marker on the map belongs to only one of these.

How a landing site is chosen

Engineers and scientists use the same short list of tests. Elevation: low ground has thicker air, which gives more braking before the engines fire; the 2021 Starship study required less than −2 km, and preferred less than −3 km, relative to the MOLA datum. Latitude: near the equator, the Sun is higher and the ground is warmer, which helps solar power; the same study required latitude below 40°. Safety: the ground must be flat, with few large rocks. Resources: a human crew would need water, and water ice is the easiest source. Science: a place with rocks that record water or possible life. These tests pull in different directions: the best-known ancient water sites are near the equator but have little ice, while the large ice deposits lie farther north and south.

The 2015 NASA workshop and “exploration zones”

In October 2015 NASA held a workshop in which researchers proposed possible landing areas for the first astronauts. Each proposal described an Exploration Zone (EZ), a circle of about 100 kilometers in radius around a landing point that contains the science targets and the resources that a crew could reach by driving (workshop abstracts, LPI Contribution 1879). Dozens of abstracts were presented. The purple circles on the map are the centers named in those abstracts, where a center was given; for several, I inferred the center from the abstract text [unconfirmed]. For two regions, Deuteronilus and Protonilus Mensae, no center was published, so the map uses the USGS center of the named region as a dashed marker. These are proposals by individual research teams. NASA has not selected any of them as the landing site for a human mission.

The proposals fall into two groups. The first is low-latitude sites with strong science: Jezero–Isidis–Syrtis, Gale, Gusev, Eastern Melas Chasma in Valles Marineris, Mawrth Vallis, Hadriacus Palus and Hellas. The second is a set of northern mid-latitude plains (Arcadia, Erebus Montes, Acheron Fossae and the Mensae regions), where earlier orbital data show ice just under the surface.

The Starship candidate sites

In 2021 a team of scientists at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, with a co-author from SpaceX, presented a study of landing sites for SpaceX’s Starship vehicle at the Lunar and Planetary Science Conference (Golombek et al., abstract 2420). Starship is meant to land very large payloads, and the authors set the tests above, plus a landing ellipse smaller than 200 meters across. They examined 22 prospective sites and listed seven as prime or secondary candidates, in Arcadia Planitia, Erebus Montes and Phlegra Montes (Figure 17). Several candidates were near ground ice, and Deuteronilus Mensae looked too rocky. Note carefully that Phlegra Montes and Arcadia Planitia were not selected by NASA as exploration zones: the Arcadia region comes from a research proposal in the 2015 workshop, and the Starship sites come from an engineering study that does not bind SpaceX or NASA.

Programs, with their status on 27 October 2026

ESA’s Rosalind Franklin rover is aimed at Oxia Planum, a plain at 18.2°N, 24.55°W (335.45°E) that ESA chose in 2018 because it has clay-rich rocks of great age. The rover will drill to a depth of 2 meters to look for organic molecules that sunlight has not destroyed. Its launch has slipped several times, and is now planned no earlier than late 2028; a landing in late 2030 has been reported [unconfirmed]. The U.S. contribution to it is not mentioned in the 2027 budget request (section 5).

China. Tianwen-1 and Zhurong landed in southern Utopia Planitia (marker on the map). The next mission, Tianwen-3, is planned to launch about 2028 and to be the first sample-return mission from Mars, according to its chief scientist Hou Zengqian, quoted by the Xinhua news agency on 4 September 2026. He said the landing site is to be finalized by the end of 2026, the mission is in the engineering-prototype stage, and China will build a planetary protection laboratory for the returned samples. Press syntheses give a return around 2031 and a short list of candidate sites; I could not confirm either, and no site is on the map [unconfirmed]. The same article gives a 1:5,000,000 geologic map of Mars, version 1.0, by the end of 2028.

Japan’s MMX launched on 20 October 2026 and aims at Phobos, not at the Martian surface. India has described a second Mars orbiter, Mangalyaan-2, for about 2030 (press report) [unconfirmed]. The UAE continues Hope’s extended mission. NASA has no human landing site approved; its listed near-term items are the budget-dependent “Mars Future Missions” program, a low-cost mission aimed at 2030, the relay orbiter, and the sample-return question. SpaceX says on its Mars page that it plans uncrewed Starship cargo flights no earlier than 2028, and in February 2026 its chief executive Elon Musk said the company would for now give priority to a city on the Moon, and that it expects to start a Mars city in about 5 to 7 years (The Guardian, 16 February 2026, quoting Musk) [aspirational]. Those are company goals. Earlier goals from the same company, a first cargo flight in 2022 and a crewed flight in 2024 (presented in 2016, from my background knowledge and not checked this session), were not met [unconfirmed].

Why it matters

A landing site is a bet that combines science, safety and survival. The sites where the best rocks are found (equator, dry) are not the sites where the ice is found (north, cold). Choosing between them decides what a first crew could do, and the proposals in this section are the first public arguments in that choice. No decision has been made.

7. People, resources and rules

What a crewed mission would involve

NASA’s main public study is Design Reference Architecture 5.0 (2009). It describes a “conjunction-class” mission, which waits for the planets to line up and stays a long time: the crew spends about 500 days on the surface and the whole mission lasts about 900 days. In its detailed 2037 example the outbound trip was 174 days, the surface stay 539 days and the return 201 days, a total of 914 days; cargo was sent two years earlier (NASA-SP-2009-566). A shorter “opposition-class” trip is possible, but needs far more fuel and a close pass of the Sun.

The most difficult problems are the following. Radiation: outside Earth’s magnetic field, a crew receives constant high-energy particles. Curiosity’s radiation detector measured about 1.84 millisieverts a day during its 253-day cruise inside the spacecraft and about 0.64 millisieverts a day on the surface (a sievert is a measure of biological dose; Hassler et al. 2014). By my own rough arithmetic, a 900-day mission would add up to about 1 sievert, with great uncertainty, because a crewed spacecraft would be shielded differently. Landing: the air is too thin for a parachute alone, and nothing as heavy as a crewed lander has yet landed; the heaviest craft landed so far weighs about one metric ton (Curiosity and Perseverance). Return: the crew must make the fuel for the trip home or carry it. Dust, cold, supplies and mental strain add more.

No agency has an approved, funded and dated crewed mission to Mars as of 27 October 2026, as far as I could find. NASA’s current language calls Mars a “horizon goal”, after the Moon (NASA release 26-025). Statements from other organizations should be read as follows. SpaceX: timelines are given in section 6 and are a company aspiration [aspirational]. China: a 2021 presentation by the state rocket maker CALT showed a crewed Mars candidate window around 2033, but it was not an approved schedule; CNSA’s 2024 roadmap is reported to place crewed Mars exploration between 2040 and 2050 [unconfirmed] [aspirational]. Cost: I did not find a recent official total for a crewed mission, so I give none. Published figures vary by an order of magnitude and depend on which parts are counted.

Making oxygen on Mars: MOXIE

Carrying everything from Earth is costly, so planners want ISRU. Perseverance carries an experiment called MOXIE (Mars Oxygen In-Situ Resource Utilization Experiment). It splits carbon dioxide, which makes up most of the Martian air, into oxygen and carbon monoxide using a hot ceramic cell. Over 16 runs it produced 122 grams of oxygen at a purity of at least 98 percent (NASA; Hoffman et al. 2022). That amount is tiny, but it shows that the process works in the real Martian air. A human mission would need a machine far larger, and the plan of making rocket fuel on Mars to return has never been tested at scale. Water ice, the other main resource, is covered by the site choices in section 6.

Planetary protection

Planetary protection means keeping Earth microbes from contaminating Mars (so that a later search for life is not fooled) and keeping any Martian material from harming Earth. The rules come from COSPAR, the international Committee on Space Research, whose policy national agencies follow. A lander that goes to Mars is in Category IV. For a lander that does not look for life, in the 2017 text I read, the whole surface may hold no more than 300,000 bacterial spores (spores are the hardy dormant form of some microbes), at no more than 300 spores per square meter on average. A mission that visits a Special Region, defined as a place where Earth microbes could grow, with water activity from 0.5 to 1.0 and a temperature of at least −28 °C, must be cleaned to a much stricter limit: no more than 30 spores on the whole landed system. Returned samples are Category V and must be contained until tested. COSPAR has revised the policy since 2017, and I did not check the current wording [unconfirmed]. A human crew cannot be sterilized, so rules for crewed missions are still being worked out. China has said it will build a planetary protection laboratory for Tianwen-3 samples (Xinhua).

The law: the Outer Space Treaty

The Outer Space Treaty of 1967 is the basic law. Article II says outer space, including the Moon and other celestial bodies, “is not subject to national appropriation by claim of sovereignty, by means of use or occupation, or by any other means”. So no country can claim Mars. Article IX requires states to explore “so as to avoid their harmful contamination”, which is the legal base of planetary protection. Article VI makes each state responsible for its national activities, including those of private companies, and requires the state to supervise them, so a company’s Mars flight needs the approval of its home state. The treaty does not say who owns materials taken from Mars; a 2015 United States law gives U.S. citizens rights to resources they obtain, and some other states say that this goes beyond the treaty [unconfirmed]. The question is open.

Key dates
  1. 1967Outer Space Treaty enters into force
  2. 2009NASA Design Reference Architecture 5.0
  3. 2021 to 2023MOXIE’s 16 runs on Mars
  4. 2017COSPAR text of the Mars rules read for this lesson
  5. 2026NASA calls Mars a “horizon goal”; no crewed mission has an approved date
Why it matters

Human exploration of Mars depends on three kinds of limits at once: engineering (radiation, landing mass, fuel), resources (water and oxygen), and rules (no ownership, and a duty to avoid contaminating the planet). Any timetable in the news should be checked against all three. Most dates given so far by companies and agencies have slipped.

Review questions

Try each one first, then open it to check the answer.

1What does the Italian word canali mean, and why were the “canals” of Mars an error?
Answer. It means “channels”. English reports turned it into “canals”, which suggests structures built by people. Lowell’s network of lines was not real: observers saw it because of blurring by Earth’s air, the eye’s habit of joining faint spots, and expectation. No spacecraft has found it.
2What did Mariner 4 find in July 1965, and how much of Mars did it photograph?
Answer. It took 21 pictures and part of a 22nd, covering about 1 percent of the surface. They showed craters like the Moon’s. It also measured a surface pressure of 4.1 to 7.0 millibars and found no magnetic field.
3Why was Mariner 9 more important than the earlier flybys?
Answer. It was the first spacecraft to orbit another planet, so it could map the whole surface over time. After a dust storm cleared, its 7,329 images revealed the giant volcanoes, the great canyon, channels and the polar caps.
4Which mission made the first soft landing on Mars, and what happened to it?
Answer. Mars 3 (USSR), on 2 December 1971. It transmitted for only seconds (14.5 to about 20 seconds in the usual accounts); the cause of the loss is unknown.
5What were the Viking biology results, and how do most scientists interpret them?
Answer. One experiment (Labeled Release) gave a signal that looked biological, but the instrument that looks for organic molecules found none. Most scientists conclude the signal was chemical. A 2010 study suggested perchlorate could have destroyed organic molecules during heating, so the question is not fully closed.
6What is MOLA, and why is it used for the maps in this course?
Answer. The Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter on Mars Global Surveyor measured the planet’s height with a laser. Its data are public and give a global elevation grid about 463 meters per pixel, so the maps can be drawn from real measurements.
7What are three tests used to choose a landing site, and why do they conflict?
Answer. Low elevation (thicker air), low latitude (warmth and sunlight), and safe, flat ground, plus access to water ice and good science. Ancient-water sites are near the equator with little ice, while the big ice deposits are farther north or south.
8What is the “potential biosignature” at Cheyava Falls, and what would settle it?
Answer. Perseverance’s Sapphire Canyon sample came from a rock with spots containing organic carbon and the minerals vivianite and greigite, arranged in a way that on Earth can result from microbes. The same minerals can form without life, though the rover found no sign of the heat or acid the non-living route would need. Bringing the sample to laboratories on Earth would be the decisive test.
9What was the state of Mars Sample Return on 27 October 2026?
Answer. No approved program. The 2023 review put the old plan at $8 to $11 billion with return about 2040; two cheaper options were studied in 2025 but none was selected. The U.S. fiscal year 2026 law does not support the existing program, and the 2027 budget request again proposes canceling it. China’s Tianwen-3 aims to launch about 2028, and Japan’s MMX plans a Phobos sample around 2031.
10What do the Outer Space Treaty’s Articles II and IX say, and how do they affect Mars?
Answer. Article II bars any country from claiming Mars or other bodies. Article IX requires states to avoid harmful contamination of other bodies, which is the legal base for planetary protection. Neither says who may own resources taken from Mars.

Data and map sources

  • Elevation: the Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) digital elevation model from Mars Global Surveyor, mosaic of 463 m per pixel (128 pixels per degree), distributed by the USGS Astrogeology Science Center (Astropedia). Public domain. Reference sphere radius 3,396,190 m. Height uncertainty is at least ±3 m, and coverage is sparse beyond 87° latitude. Colors and shading were computed from the data for this lesson.
  • Coordinates: planetocentric latitude, east-positive longitude measured from the Airy-0 crater, on a plain equirectangular grid. Regional maps compress the horizontal scale by the cosine of a stated latitude. No map is an equal-area map. One degree of arc on Mars is about 59.27 km.
  • Interactive tool, not a source for the maps: NASA/JPL Mars Trek, trek.nasa.gov/mars, offers its own MOLA-based layers, landing-site markers, a Perseverance path layer and exploration-zone layers. The maps in this course were built from the data sources listed here, not from Mars Trek.
  • Landing sites: NASA GISS Mars24 “Mars Lander Missions” list (updated 9 December 2023), checked against NSSDCA records for Viking 1; Mars 2 and 3 are approximate. Newer sites were checked against mission pages.
  • Perseverance route: NASA/JPL Mars 2020 MMGIS traverse and waypoint data, retrieved 27 October 2026; the last point used is sol 2009 (about 45.2 km from the start at sol 13).
  • Future sites: positions are read from the figures and text of the abstracts named in each caption. Where an abstract gave no center, the center is my estimate and is marked approximate. The USGS Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature gives region centers; a region center is not a landing site.
  • Dates and numbers: every figure is attributed in the text. Items I could not confirm against a source other than Wikipedia, or confirm in a second source, are marked [unconfirmed]; company and national timelines are marked [aspirational]. Budget requests are proposals, and Congress decides the final amounts.
